task.goal: Help first-time visitors use a walk-in neighborhood legal-information desk without making them disclose private details in the waiting area.
hard_constraints: Two volunteers have one desk and printed public information; they do not give legal advice.
No app, registration requirement or public triage of personal cases.
Check successful navigation, waiting confusion and privacy complaints.
task.available_resources: Existing opening hours, printed service scope and a quiet corner.
task.expected_result: An inclusive first-visit flow with escalation to qualified help.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Anonymous turn queue with a private orientation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Make arrival and waiting independent of a visitor’s legal issue. Put a short welcome sheet at the desk stating opening hours, service scope, “legal information, not legal advice,” and “You do not need to explain your situation while waiting.” Visitors take the next numbered paper slip; no name, registration or case description is requested. One volunteer manages turns and explains the process without asking why anyone came. The other offers each visitor a brief orientation in the quiet corner. Visitors can speak, point to printed information or ask the volunteer to read it aloud. They may decline to share details altogether. After orientation, they receive relevant public information or directions to qualified help using referral details already present in the materials. Volunteers explain their limits before discussing any question and do not interpret facts, recommend legal action or predict outcomes. The mechanism is predictable access: visitors secure a place without disclosing a reason, reducing pressure to explain themselves publicly. Implementation needs handwritten slips, a visible current number and consistent volunteer wording. Read numbers aloud and display them so neither hearing nor reading alone is necessary. Assume the quiet corner permits conversation without ordinary waiting-area audibility; inspect this first. If it does not, use it only for general orientation and explain that confidential discussion is unavailable. Limits include slower service when every visitor needs orientation, possible number confusion and referrals constrained by the supplied information.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the prototype with a simple welcome-and-wait instruction in short role-play sessions with first-time users. Ask participants to join the queue, identify their turn, locate service limits and find the route to qualified help without revealing a case. Record unaided completion, questions about waiting and anonymous privacy complaints or concerns. Use fictional situations only. Reject or revise the design if numbering adds confusion, anyone believes disclosure is required to obtain a turn, or ordinary speech from the corner is intelligible in the waiting area. This checks usability and exposure, not legal outcomes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Visitor-controlled information route
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Let visitors begin with public information independently, with human assistance available by choice. Arrange the existing materials into a short, numbered route: first read the desk’s scope and hours; next browse information; finally choose whether to leave with materials or request a quiet conversation. A plain-language welcome sheet explains that browsing does not require approaching the desk, giving a name or describing a problem. Keep document titles facing the visitor where feasible and do not create separate topic queues or ask people to display their selections. One volunteer offers neutral orientation and reading assistance; the other handles requested conversations in the quiet corner. People requesting conversation receive anonymous turn slips and may wait without holding topic-specific material. A visitor can point privately to a passage instead of narrating personal circumstances. Volunteers explain public information and service boundaries; questions requiring application of law to personal facts are directed to qualified help identified in the available materials. The mechanism is visitor control over whether and when interaction occurs: some first visits can succeed without any case discussion, leaving volunteer time for those needing assistance. Setup requires a one-page route, ordered stacks of existing printouts and a clear place to request assistance. It assumes the materials are understandable enough to support independent use and contain usable referral information. Reading difficulty, limited language coverage and difficulty browsing physically may limit independence, so volunteers must offer assistance without making self-service a prerequisite. Document selection may itself reveal a concern; this approach reduces compelled disclosure but cannot guarantee privacy in a shared room.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the numbered route with the same printouts in an unstructured stack. Give first-time participants fictional goals, including finding opening hours, understanding service limits and reaching qualified help. Include participants who prefer spoken assistance. Observe unaided navigation, uncertainty about whether to wait and privacy concerns about browsing or requesting help. Collect feedback without names or case details. Revise if users mistake browsing for a required step, cannot find human assistance or feel their topic is exposed. A small check can identify failures but cannot establish accessibility across all languages or needs.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Short welcome rounds followed by private individual turns
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Replace repeated public arrival conversations with a brief, recurring explanation of the service. At opening and between individual turns, one volunteer gives a short welcome covering what the desk provides, what volunteers cannot do, how waiting works and how to reach qualified help. Explicitly say that nobody should describe a personal case during the welcome and that attendance is optional. Display the same explanation in print for late arrivals and people who prefer reading. Visitors can join an anonymous numbered queue immediately; missing the welcome never delays access. The second volunteer conducts individual information conversations in the quiet corner. The welcoming volunteer handles only operational questions in the waiting area and redirects attempted personal disclosures gently: “You can keep those details for your individual turn.” Offer individual reading or explanation of the welcome when needed. At the private turn, visitors can request general information without giving personal details. Questions requiring legal judgment receive a clear boundary statement and directions to qualified assistance already listed in the materials. The mechanism is shared expectation-setting: everyone hears the same privacy boundary and waiting instructions before uncertainty prompts a public explanation of their case. It requires a short script, printed equivalent, handwritten turn slips and coordination between two volunteers. Assume brief announcements will not interrupt quiet-corner conversations or expose them; positioning must be checked. Limits include repetitive announcements, language and hearing barriers, and the possibility that a group setting discourages some visitors. Qualified referrals remain dependent on the accuracy and coverage of existing printouts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a fictional arrival exercise comparing the welcome-round format with giving the same explanation separately to each arrival. Include someone arriving halfway through a welcome and someone declining group participation. Check whether participants can identify their next step, understand the wait and locate escalation to qualified help. Count waiting-related clarification requests and invite anonymous privacy complaints. Revise if late arrivals are disadvantaged, anyone thinks attendance is compulsory, personal disclosures occur during the welcome or announcements interfere with private conversations. Treat any apparent improvement as preliminary until checked during ordinary service without collecting case details.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Case-free questions with a direct route to qualified help
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the desk useful without collecting anyone’s personal account. The primary mechanism is information minimization: volunteers help visitors navigate published information, while questions requiring personal facts move to qualified help instead of becoming volunteer case discussions. This reduces dependence on the quiet corner being confidential.

At arrival, display the existing hours and service scope alongside a short instruction: “No name or personal story needed. We can help you find public information and contact details for qualified help.” Offer three neutral requests visitors can say or point to: “Explain this service,” “Help me understand this leaflet,” and “Help me find qualified assistance.” All requests use the same waiting process, so choosing assistance does not create a visible case category. Use anonymous paper turns, with numbers both shown and spoken.

One volunteer handles arrival and waiting questions. The second provides individual assistance in the quiet corner, first explaining that it may not be confidential. Visitors can ask about a published term or passage without describing their circumstances. If someone begins recounting a case, gently interrupt before further details: “You can keep those details private. We can explain the printed information or show you how to contact qualified help.” Volunteers do not reformulate a personal account into a legal question, select a legal strategy or assess urgency from case facts.

Implementation needs a short printed request card, paper turns and rehearsal of the boundary wording. It assumes the existing materials contain current, usable referral details; inspect these first. If they do not, escalation remains an unresolved service gap. Limits include reduced usefulness for visitors unable to separate general questions from their circumstances, possible feelings of rejection, and no guarantee that visitors will avoid spontaneous disclosure.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this flow with ordinary private orientation in a small role-play using fictional situations. Ask first-time participants to find information, understand waiting and identify how to reach qualified help. Include someone who starts telling a personal story and someone needing spoken assistance. Record navigation completion, waiting clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints or concerns. Also check whether redirection feels respectful and whether participants mistake public information for advice about their case. Revise or reject if the boundary prevents useful assistance, referral instructions cannot be followed, or personal disclosures remain as frequent as in the comparator. This tests usability and disclosure prevention, not referral availability or legal outcomes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Separate the waiting boundary from the information conversation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use physical separation to keep ordinary service conversations out of the waiting area. The mechanism is controlling where people wait and approach: visitors obtain access without explaining their purpose, and individual assistance begins only after the previous visitor has left the conversation space.

Before adopting this layout, test whether the desk can face the quiet corner while a waiting position elsewhere in the existing space remains outside ordinary conversational hearing. Keep a clear, accessible route between them. If that separation is impossible, this alternative does not work; a quiet corner alone is not evidence of privacy.

Place the existing opening hours and service scope at the waiting boundary, with a plain instruction: “Please wait here. You do not need to explain why you came. A volunteer will welcome you.” One volunteer stays near this boundary, offers spoken or pointing-based assistance and maintains arrival order without names or case categories. The other uses the desk beside the quiet corner for one visitor or visitor-chosen companion group at a time. The welcoming volunteer escorts people who need help reaching their turn; standing in a line is not required.

At the desk, explain that volunteers provide public legal information, not legal advice, and that personal details are optional. Help visitors use the printed materials and locate qualified assistance already listed there. Do not interpret their circumstances or recommend legal action.

Implementation requires repositioning the existing desk and printouts, a paper boundary sign and coordination between the two volunteers. It assumes sufficient accessible space and usable referral information in the materials. Nearby conversations, crowding and companions can still compromise privacy; the layout must not be described as confidential. Missing referral details remain an unresolved escalation gap.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this layout with waiting immediately beside the desk, using fictional questions and a few first-time participants. Ask visitors to arrive, wait, obtain a leaflet and identify the route to qualified help. Record successful navigation, waiting-related clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints or concerns. Have a participant at the waiting boundary report whether they can understand ordinary-volume conversation at the desk. Reject the layout if speech is intelligible, arrivals routinely cross the boundary prematurely, or visitors needing seating or mobility assistance lose their place. This checks the proposed spatial protection, not confidentiality under every operating condition.

EXPAND.title: A complete first-visit packet without a case conversation
EXPAND.proposal:
Make a successful first visit possible through a single, identical packet containing the existing service scope, opening hours, public information and available directions to qualified help. The mechanism is removing a presumed prerequisite: visitors need neither identify a legal topic nor complete an orientation to receive the desk’s information. Identical packets also avoid revealing interests through visible document selection.

Before opening, the two volunteers assemble a manageable set from existing printouts, keeping scope and referral instructions at the front. At entry, one volunteer says, “You can take this without giving your name or explaining anything. Assistance is optional.” Visitors may leave immediately, read, or wait for assistance in arrival order. The second volunteer offers help in the quiet corner, including reading aloud when privacy permits. Taking or understanding the packet is never a condition of assistance.

For questions, volunteers explain published information without applying law to personal circumstances. Requests for interpretation or recommendations go to qualified services actually identified in the materials. If the packet lacks a suitable referral, say that the desk cannot identify one from its resources; do not imply that the packet resolves the issue.

This needs sufficient existing copies and a packet small enough to use. It assumes the materials contain a usable route to qualified help. Broad packets may overwhelm readers, waste paper or expose sensitive topics after visitors leave; offer loose sheets privately if requested. Compared with the prior browsing route, this removes the need to select a topic or approach a volunteer, but may increase reading burden.
EXPAND.experiment: One volunteer owns a six-person fictional first-visit trial comparing identical packets with the prior optional browsing route using the same materials. Include visitors needing spoken assistance. Check successful departure with usable information or a correctly identified qualified-help route, waiting clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints. Also count pages distributed and time needed to find the relevant next step. Stop and revise if anyone believes reading is required for assistance, cannot obtain help, or mistakes the packet for legal advice. Prefer the packet only if reduced interaction or exposure outweighs added search effort; this small trial cannot establish broad accessibility.

EXPAND.title: A quiet-corner channel that does not depend on quiet speech
EXPAND.proposal:
Protect the individual exchange by changing its communication channel when the corner cannot provide acoustic privacy. A quiet location alone does not establish confidentiality. Before opening, volunteers check whether ordinary conversation there is intelligible from the waiting area. The desk then offers a silent exchange on paper as an equal option, with spoken service limited to information visitors are comfortable having overheard.

At entry, one volunteer gives only scope, hours and waiting instructions, explicitly saying no case explanation is needed. Visitors wait in arrival order without names or topic labels. The second volunteer meets them in the corner and offers writing, pointing to existing public information, or general spoken explanation. A sheet positioned out of waiting-area sight says: “Please ask a general question. Names, addresses and case documents are unnecessary.” Volunteers request no personal history and interrupt unnecessary identifying detail before it accumulates.

The volunteer supplies relevant printed information or writes directions to qualified help already listed in the materials. Questions requiring application of law to individual facts receive a written boundary statement and referral. At the end, the visitor takes every written exchange; volunteers keep no copy. If the visitor cannot use writing or pointing and speech would expose details, continue with general information and explain the available qualified-help route without requesting disclosure.

Resources are existing printouts, their blank reverse sides, a pen and positioning that prevents casual reading. These modest stationery needs must be available. Compared with private orientation, the mechanism addresses overhearing directly. It can slow service and exclude people with visual, literacy or dexterity barriers, and it cannot promise privacy from someone deliberately looking over a shoulder.
EXPAND.experiment: The corner volunteer owns a short trial comparing written exchanges with the prior spoken orientation, using fictional questions and identical referral materials. Include a participant who cannot comfortably write. Observe whether waiting-area listeners can recover any fictional detail, whether visitors reach an appropriate information or referral endpoint, waiting confusion, anonymous privacy complaints and service time. Stop the written trial if sheets are visible to waiting visitors, visitors leave unwanted written records behind, or someone loses access because writing becomes compulsory. Reject it as the default if privacy gains come with unacceptable access failures; retain it only as an optional channel if that performs better.

EXPAND.title: A visitor-rehearsed handoff to qualified help
EXPAND.proposal:
Make escalation usable by rehearsing the next access step before the visitor leaves. Giving a referral may fail when visitors cannot tell whom to contact, how to approach the service or what to do if access fails. This route changes that final link without collecting case facts or requiring the desk to contact anyone.

At entry, one volunteer explains the desk’s limits and arrival-order waiting: visitors need not state a reason or name. The second volunteer provides individual assistance in the quiet corner, using only questions about the public information requested. Visitors may receive materials and leave without discussion. If they need legal judgment, the volunteer explains the boundary and identifies qualified assistance only where the existing materials support it.

With the visitor’s agreement, the volunteer marks the referral’s published contact method, hours and any stated access conditions on the visitor’s copy. They ask, “Would you like to show me where you would start?” The visitor can point, explain or decline; this is assistance, never an eligibility test. Resolve uncertainty by rereading the source together. Mark a fallback only if another applicable route is actually documented. Where hours, eligibility or availability are absent, label them unknown and explain that the receiving service must confirm them. Visitors may return during desk hours for further help understanding the printed instructions, without repeating personal details.

This needs a pen, current referral information and volunteer time. Assume at least one qualified-help route exists in the materials; otherwise the desk must acknowledge the gap. Compared with private orientation followed by directions, rehearsal can reveal access misunderstandings, but adds time and cannot establish that a service will answer, accept the visitor or provide representation.
EXPAND.experiment: One volunteer owns an eight-scenario role-play comparing a standard printed referral with the same referral plus optional rehearsal. Include a closed service and incomplete eligibility information. Check whether participants can demonstrate their next contact step, distinguish confirmed information from unknowns and recover using a documented fallback where available. Record waiting clarification requests, anonymous privacy complaints, consultation duration and queue delay. Stop if rehearsal pressures anyone to disclose facts or volunteers invent access conditions. Reject the addition if correct navigation does not improve enough to justify delay. Report demonstrated navigation separately from actual access to qualified help, which this trial cannot establish.

EXPAND.title: Anonymous queue with a privacy-preserving interruption procedure
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Anonymous turn queue with a private orientation,” selected for its direct protection of arrival privacy and modest daily burden. Preserve anonymous numbered slips, visible and spoken turn calls, optional quiet-corner orientation, reading assistance, public information and escalation to qualified help documented in the materials. No name or case explanation is needed to join or retain a turn.

The changed action addresses interruptions: the arrival volunteer owns the queue; the corner volunteer owns the current conversation until it ends or is explicitly paused. If either volunteer must leave their role, pause new individual conversations rather than having the remaining volunteer manage arrivals while discussing someone’s question. Tell the current visitor privately that service is paused, return their materials and preserve their turn. Announce only that individual assistance is temporarily paused. On resumption, offer the interrupted visitor the next turn without asking them to repeat details publicly. If they cannot stay, provide available public information and documented qualified-help contacts, explaining that a later visit may involve waiting again.

Before opening, the corner volunteer checks whether ordinary conversation is intelligible from the waiting position. If it is, offer only general information there and explain the privacy limitation before inviting questions. Volunteers never apply law to personal facts or promise confidentiality the room cannot provide.

Resources are the existing printouts and corner, plus paper slips, a pen and a current-number display. The mechanism remains predictable anonymous access; the upgrade prevents staffing interruptions from undoing that protection. It adds pauses and potentially longer waits, but requires no personal records. Referral usefulness remains dependent on the supplied materials.
EXPAND.experiment: The arrival volunteer leads a short fictional first-visit rehearsal comparing the original numbered flow with the interruption procedure. Include a late arrival, a visitor needing spoken instructions, an interruption during assistance and an interrupted visitor who must leave. Test a general request for published service hours, a request to calculate a personal legal deadline and an unfamiliar topic absent from the materials. Check successful navigation to information or an honestly bounded qualified-help route, waiting clarification requests, anonymous privacy complaints, pause duration and repeated explanations. Inspect audibility from the waiting position. Stop individual discussion immediately if fictional details become intelligible there or role coverage breaks down; use general information until corrected. Retain the upgrade only if interruption recovery improves without making waiting materially harder to understand. This rehearsal cannot establish actual access to qualified help.

EXPAND.title: A general-information desk with no personal-case intake
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a different primary mechanism: remove personal-case intake from the entire visit. Privacy then depends less on finding a confidential place to explain a situation. At the existing arrival contact, one volunteer says, “You can use this desk without telling us what happened. We explain published information; questions about what you should do need qualified help.” Visitors may take information, request reading assistance or wait anonymously in arrival order. Display and speak the same short waiting instructions.

The second volunteer answers questions about the printed material without inviting a narrative. Visitors may point to a passage or ask a general question; they are never required to reformulate a personal story to receive help. If someone begins disclosing details, the volunteer gently interrupts: “You don’t need to give those details here.” Offer to explain a relevant publication, show the available qualified-help contacts or let the visitor leave with materials. Use the quiet corner for less exposed reading and explanation, but do not describe it as confidential.

The decision boundary is whether an answer can be given directly from public information without judging the visitor’s circumstances. Volunteers may explain a published contact method or service scope. They do not decide how a rule applies, recommend action or predict outcomes. When the boundary is reached, the assisting volunteer shows the documented referral instructions before ending the exchange. If interrupted, return the visitor’s materials and preserve their place for completion. If no suitable qualified-help route is documented, explicitly acknowledge the gap rather than selecting an unsupported destination.

This needs the existing scope, hours, printouts and two volunteers; a short handwritten welcome and anonymous turn markers require basic stationery. It assumes some useful general information and referral instructions exist. Compared with private orientation, it removes the expectation of telling a case and can operate despite poor acoustic privacy. The shifted cost is reduced tailoring and more navigation work for visitors. Spoken assistance remains available, but language coverage and the quality of printed referrals remain limitations.
EXPAND.experiment: The assisting volunteer owns a bounded rehearsal of six fictional visits comparing this no-intake procedure with the anonymous queue and private orientation. Include someone who assumes disclosure is compulsory, someone needing reading assistance and someone who starts a personal narrative. Test a published opening-hours question, a request to apply a rule to personal facts and an unfamiliar issue absent from the printouts. Record successful navigation, waiting confusion, anonymous privacy complaints, unnecessary disclosures, time spent and whether visitors can identify a usable next step. Stop and correct the procedure if volunteers solicit case facts, give individualized advice or withhold assistance because a visitor cannot frame a general question. Reject it as the main flow if reduced disclosure comes with more visitors leaving without understandable information or an honestly explained referral gap. No trial result is assumed.
